set.detail: Titus Flavius Vespasianus was born on 17 November 9 at Falacrinae near Reate in Sabine country, son of a tax collector and banker of equestrian rank; his mother's family had senatorial connections. He rose slowly through the senatorial career with help from Antonia's freedwoman Caenis, his lifelong companion, and Claudius's freedman Narcissus, and won fame as legate of II Augusta in the conquest of Britain (43-47), fighting thirty battles and taking the Isle of Wight and over twenty hillforts, for which he received triumphal ornaments and the consulship of 51. He governed Africa, where he was pelted with turnips and became so poor he traded mules, accompanied Nero to Greece in 66 and fell from favour for dozing during the emperor's recitals, but was appointed in 67 to suppress the Jewish revolt, perhaps because his humble origins made him no threat. He reduced Galilee and most of Judaea by 68. Proclaimed emperor at Alexandria on 1 July 69, he won the civil war through the Danube legions and Mucianus and reached Rome in 70. As emperor (69-79) he restored order and finances, raising taxes vigorously (hence the urine tax), reorganised the eastern frontier and annexed Commagene, granted Latin rights to Spain, held the censorship (73-74), enrolled new senators from Italy and the provinces, and built the Temple of Peace and the Colosseum, restored the Capitol and completed the temple of Claudius. He established a new dynasty, insisting "either my sons will succeed me or no one will", and associated Titus closely in power. His humour was earthy and his manner affable; his last words were reportedly "Alas, I think I am becoming a god", and, trying to rise, "an emperor should die standing". He died of fever and diarrhoea at Aquae Cutiliae on 23 June 79. The sources are generally favourable, and modern historians (Levick) regard him as one of the most effective emperors, the restorer of the Principate after 68-69.

Titus Flavius Vespasianus, Vespasian's elder son, born on 30 December 39, was educated at court with Britannicus, beside whom he was dining when Britannicus was poisoned. He served as military tribune in Germany and Britain and commanded XV Apollinaris under his father in Judaea, taking Tarichaeae, Gamala and Gischala. He brokered the alliance of Vespasian and Mucianus in 69 and was left to finish the Jewish war, capturing Jerusalem in 70 after a five-month siege and destroying the Temple. He celebrated the triumph with his father in 71 and became his colleague in power, holding tribunician power, seven consulships, the censorship and the praetorian prefecture, in which role he gained a reputation for ruthlessness, killing the consular Caecina Alienus at dinner on suspicion of conspiracy. His affair with the Jewish queen Berenice, who lived with him on the Palatine, caused scandal, and he sent her away. Becoming emperor on 24 June 79, he reinvented himself as the "delight and darling of the human race" (amor ac deliciae generis humani), refusing to sign death warrants and expelling informers. His brief reign was marked by disasters: the eruption of Vesuvius (79), a three-day fire in Rome and an epidemic (80), to which he responded with generous relief. He inaugurated the Colosseum with a hundred days of games and built the Baths of Titus. Suetonius records his saying, on a day when he had given no gift, "friends, I have lost a day". He died of fever on 13 September 81 at the family villa near Reate, aged 41, reportedly saying that he had only one regret; rumours accused Domitian of hastening his death. Rabbinic legend attributed it to a gnat that entered his brain as punishment for destroying the Temple. He was deified, and the Arch of Titus commemorates his apotheosis and triumph. Modern historians note that his popularity owed much to the brevity of his reign and the contrast with Domitian.

Titus Flavius Domitianus, younger son of Vespasian, born on 24 October 51, was in Rome during the civil war of 69, escaped the burning of the Capitol disguised as a follower of Isis, and was briefly acting ruler before Mucianus arrived. Under his father and brother he was kept in honorific roles and devoted himself to poetry. Emperor from 81 to 96, he ruled with great energy and personal control. He campaigned against the Chatti (83), annexing the Taunus and building the Upper German limes; organised the provinces of Upper and Lower Germany; fought the Dacians after their invasion of Moesia (85-89), losing Oppius Sabinus and Cornelius Fuscus but winning at Tapae (88) and making a peace in 89 that paid Decebalus subsidies; and fought the Suebi and Sarmatians (89-92). He crushed the revolt of Antonius Saturninus (89). He raised army pay by a third, improved the silver content of the coinage (82) before reducing it (85), held the censorship for life, enforced moral legislation, executed Vestals, rebuilt the Capitol and built a huge palace on the Palatine, the Stadium, the Odeum, the Forum Transitorium and a villa at Alba. Administration in the provinces was strict and effective; Suetonius admits that governors had never been more honest. His relations with the Senate were poor: he was suspicious, autocratic and sarcastic, styled "lord and god" by flatterers, and after 93 executed many senators, including the Stoic circle around Helvidius Priscus the Younger and Arulenus Rusticus, and expelled philosophers. He was murdered by his court on 18 September 96. The Senate condemned his memory, and the writers of the next generation, Tacitus, Pliny and Juvenal, painted him as a tyrant, but the army mourned him. Modern historians (Jones, Southern) present him as a capable, hardworking ruler whose autocratic style alienated the elite.

Yosef ben Matityahu, born in Jerusalem in 37/38 to a priestly family related through his mother to the Hasmoneans, studied with the Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and the hermit Bannus, and in 64 went to Rome to secure the release of priests sent there by Felix, gaining access to Poppaea. In 66 the revolutionary government appointed him general in Galilee, where he fortified towns, clashed with John of Gischala and was besieged at Jotapata by Vespasian in 67. After the fall of the town he hid in a cave with forty men who agreed to kill each other by lot; Josephus survived, by luck or manipulation, surrendered and predicted that Vespasian would become emperor. Freed in 69, he took the name Titus Flavius Josephus, served Titus as interpreter during the siege of Jerusalem and pleaded with the defenders to surrender, earning the hatred of both sides. After the war he lived in Rome on a pension in Vespasian's former house, with Roman citizenship and estates in Judaea. He wrote the Jewish War (seven books, c. 75-79, first in Aramaic then Greek), the Jewish Antiquities (twenty books, 93/94), an autobiography (Life) defending his conduct in Galilee against Justus of Tiberias, and Against Apion, a defence of Judaism. His works are the main source for Jewish history from the Maccabees to 74, Herod, the procurators, the revolt and Masada, and contain the notices of John the Baptist, James and Jesus. He married four times. Jews long regarded him as a traitor, while Christians preserved his works for their testimony to Christ and to the punishment of Jerusalem. Modern scholarship (Rajak, Mason) reads him as a sophisticated author with his own apologetic agenda, defending both the Flavians and the Jewish people, and blaming the revolt on a small group of brigands and tyrants. He died around 100.

Gnaeus Julius Agricola was born on 13 June 40 at Forum Julii (Fréjus) in Narbonensis, into a family of senatorial rank; his father Julius Graecinus was executed by Caligula. Educated at Massilia, he served as military tribune in Britain under Suetonius Paullinus during the Boudican revolt, was quaestor in Asia, tribune and praetor under Nero, and in 69 lost his mother to Othonian marines who plundered the family estates in Liguria. He joined Vespasian early and commanded XX Valeria Victrix in Britain (70-73) under Petillius Cerialis. He was adlected to the patriciate, governed Aquitania (74-76), and was consul in 76 or 77, when he betrothed his daughter to Tacitus. As governor of Britain for an unusually long term (77/78 to 83/84), he completed the conquest of Wales, encouraged towns, baths and Roman education among the British elite, advanced through northern England into Scotland, reaching the Tay, consolidating the Forth-Clyde line, considering an invasion of Ireland, and defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius in 83 or 84. His fleet sailed round the north of Britain. Domitian recalled him, granting triumphal ornaments and a statue but no further appointment, and he declined to draw lots for Asia or Africa. He died on 23 August 93, with rumours of poison that Tacitus reports but does not endorse. Almost everything known about him comes from Tacitus's biography (98), an encomium which presents him as a model of the good man under a bad emperor, quietly serving the state without seeking glory or provoking martyrdom. Archaeology (the forts and marching camps of Scotland, the Verulamium forum inscription and inscribed lead water pipes from Chester naming him) confirms the broad outline, but scholars debate how much of the Flavian advance should be credited to his predecessors Cerialis and Frontinus. A fragmentary inscription from Verulamium (79) bears his name.

Publius (or Gaius) Cornelius Tacitus was born c. 56, probably in Narbonensis or northern Italy, perhaps son of an equestrian procurator of Belgica mentioned by Pliny. Trained in oratory in Rome, he married Agricola's daughter in 77 and began a senatorial career under Vespasian, advanced by Titus and Domitian; he was praetor and quindecimvir in 88, served in the provinces from 89 to 93, and was in Rome during the terror of Domitian's last years, which he describes with personal shame. He was consul suffect in 97 under Nerva, delivering the funeral oration for Verginius Rufus, prosecuted Marius Priscus with Pliny in 100, and was proconsul of Asia c. 112-113, according to an inscription from Mylasa. His works are the Agricola and the Germania (98), the Dialogue on Orators (c. 102), the Histories (covering 69-96, of which Books 1-4 and part of 5 survive, ending in 70) and the Annals (from the death of Augustus to Nero, of which Books 1-6, partly, and 11-16, partly, survive). He promised to write "sine ira et studio" (without anger or partisanship) but his narrative is shaped by a bleak view of the Principate, a fascination with the corruption of power and the moral compromises of the aristocracy, and a style of extreme concision, variation and innuendo. He used senatorial records (acta senatus), memoirs (of Agrippina, Corbulo, Suetonius Paullinus) and earlier historians such as Pliny the Elder, Cluvius Rufus and Fabius Rusticus. His accuracy has been confirmed in many details by documents such as the Lyon tablet and the SC de Cn. Pisone patre, though the latter also shows his selective emphasis. Almost forgotten in late antiquity, his works survived in two Monte Cassino and Fulda manuscripts. He influenced Machiavelli, Montaigne and political thought of the early modern period and remains the greatest Roman historian in the judgement of many, including Syme, who wrote his monumental biography (1958).

Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus was born at Comum (Como) in 61/62, son of Lucius Caecilius Cilo and nephew of Pliny the Elder, who adopted him in his will after dying at Vesuvius in 79, an event the 17-year-old witnessed from Misenum and later described for Tacitus. He studied rhetoric with Quintilian and became a leading advocate in the centumviral court, where he pleaded inheritance cases. His senatorial career, under Domitian, Nerva and Trajan, included the prefecture of the military treasury (94-96) and of the treasury of Saturn (98-100), the consulship (suffect, September 100), when he delivered the Panegyricus to Trajan, the augurate and the curatorship of the Tiber (104-106). He prosecuted provincial governors for extortion, including Marius Priscus with Tacitus. Around 110 Trajan sent him as legate with consular power to Bithynia and Pontus to sort out municipal finances; he died there c. 112-113. His nine books of literary letters, published in stages, offer a portrait of the senatorial elite of the period: villas at Laurentum and in Tuscany, literary recitations, patronage, legacies, his three marriages and his affection for his young wife Calpurnia, the ghost of Athens, the dolphin of Hippo, and the eruption of Vesuvius. The tenth book contains his official correspondence with Trajan, including requests for advice on a fire brigade for Nicomedia, aqueducts, a canal and the treatment of Christians (Letter 10.96), with Trajan's replies. An inscription from Comum lists his career and his benefactions, including a library, an alimentary fund for children and baths, totalling over five million sesterces. He has been criticised for vanity and complacency, but his letters are an incomparable source for social history and for the relationship between emperor and governor.

Decebalus, king of the Dacians from c. 87, possibly the successor of Duras, was the most capable enemy Rome faced on the Danube in the first century. In 85-86 the Dacians invaded Moesia and killed the governor Oppius Sabinus, and in 86 or 87 destroyed the army of the praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus. Defeated by Tettius Julianus at Tapae (88), Decebalus negotiated a peace in 89 with Domitian, who needed his troops against the Marcomanni and Quadi. Under its terms Decebalus became a client king, receiving an annual subsidy, Roman engineers and craftsmen, which he used to strengthen his fortresses in the Orastie mountains around Sarmizegetusa Regia. Dio describes him as shrewd in war, skilled in ambushes and in knowing when to retreat. Trajan regarded the treaty as humiliating and in 101 invaded Dacia. In the first war (101-102) the Romans won a hard battle at Tapae and Decebalus's counter-offensive into Moesia was defeated at Adamclisi; he accepted harsh terms, giving up territory, engineers, deserters and weapons, and his sister was captured. He soon rearmed, attacked the Iazyges and in 105 captured the Roman commander Pompeius Longinus, sent assassins against Trajan and attacked Roman garrisons. In the second war (105-106) Trajan, crossing on the new bridge at Drobeta, took Sarmizegetusa; Decebalus fled north and, when a Roman cavalry patrol led by Tiberius Claudius Maximus overtook him, cut his own throat. Maximus carried his head and right hand to Trajan at Ranisstorum, and they were displayed on the Gemonian steps in Rome. Maximus's tombstone found at Grammeni in Macedonia (1965) shows the scene, as does Trajan's Column. His treasure, hidden in the river Sargetia, was revealed by his companion Bicilis. In modern Romanian national tradition Decebalus is a hero of resistance, commemorated by a 40 m rock carving of his face on the Danube at the Iron Gates (1994-2004).

Marcus Ulpius Traianus was born on 18 September 53 at Italica in Baetica, son of a distinguished general of the same name who commanded X Fretensis in the Jewish war, was consul under Vespasian, governor of Syria and patrician. The younger Trajan served for ten years as military tribune, commanded VII Gemina in Spain, marched it to the Rhine against Saturninus in 89, was consul in 91 and governor of Upper Germany when Nerva adopted him in October 97. Emperor from January 98, he stayed on the frontier until 99 and won a reputation as the "best princeps" (optimus, officially part of his titulature from 114) through his respect for the Senate, accessibility and modest lifestyle, while firmly holding power. He conquered Dacia in two wars (101-102, 105-106), creating a province rich in gold, and annexed the Nabataean kingdom as the province of Arabia (106). The Dacian spoils financed his Forum, Column, Markets and Baths, the harbour at Portus, the Via Traiana and the alimenta for poor Italian children. His correspondence with Pliny shows a careful administrator. In 113 he launched a war against Parthia, annexing Armenia (114), Mesopotamia (115) and reaching the Persian Gulf after taking Ctesiphon (116), but revolts in the new territories and among the Jewish diaspora in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia forced a retreat. He died at Selinus in Cilicia in August 117, and Hadrian, whose adoption was disputed, succeeded and gave up the eastern conquests. Dio notes his fondness for wine and boys, but considered them harmless. Late antique senators acclaimed new emperors with the wish that they be "luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan", and a medieval legend held that Pope Gregory's prayers saved his soul. Modern historians debate his motives for the Parthian war, from glory-seeking (Dio's view) to strategic or commercial aims.

Publius Aelius Hadrianus, born on 24 January 76, probably in Rome, to a family from Italica related to Trajan, was orphaned at ten and became the ward of Trajan and Acilius Attianus. His love of Greek culture earned him the nickname "Graeculus". He served as military tribune in three legions, carried the news of Nerva's death to Trajan, married Trajan's grand-niece Vibia Sabina in 100 with Plotina's support, commanded I Minervia in the Second Dacian War, was archon at Athens (112) and governor of Syria when Trajan died. Emperor from August 117, he abandoned Trajan's eastern conquests and spent more than half his reign travelling through the provinces (121-125 and 128-132), inspecting armies, building frontier works including the Wall in Britain and the palisade in Germany, founding cities (Antinoopolis, Hadrianopolis) and showering benefactions, especially on Athens, where he completed the Olympieion and founded the Panhellenion. He reformed administration, placing equestrians in the palace bureaus, codified the praetor's edict through Salvius Julianus, extended the consilium and protected slaves from abuse. In Rome he built the Pantheon, the Temple of Venus and Roma (to his own design, which Apollodorus mocked, allegedly at the cost of his life), his Mausoleum and the Villa at Tibur. His beloved Antinous drowned in the Nile in 130 and was deified. The Bar Kokhba revolt (132-136), provoked by his foundation of Aelia Capitolina or a ban on circumcision, was suppressed with great loss. His relations with the Senate were tense from the execution of four consulars in 118 to the forced suicide of his brother-in-law Servianus and his grand-nephew Fuscus in 136. Ill in his last years, he adopted Lucius Aelius Caesar (136) and after his death Antoninus (138), who was to adopt Marcus and Lucius. He died at Baiae on 10 July 138, composing the poem "animula vagula blandula". Modern biographers (Birley) stress his restlessness, intellect, curiosity and capacity for cruelty.

Titus Aurelius Fulvus Boionius Arrius Antoninus was born on 19 September 86 at Lanuvium, from a wealthy senatorial family of Nemausus in Narbonensis. He was consul in 120, one of the four consulars appointed by Hadrian to administer justice in Italy, and proconsul of Asia (c. 134-135), where he was known for fairness. In February 138, after the death of Lucius Aelius, Hadrian adopted him on condition that he in turn adopt Marcus Annius Verus (Marcus Aurelius) and Lucius Ceionius Commodus (Lucius Verus). Emperor from July 138 to March 161, he forced the reluctant Senate to deify Hadrian and received the name Pius. His 23-year reign, the most peaceful in Roman history, was marked by careful finance, respect for the Senate, mild justice and the absence of major wars, apart from the advance in Britain to the Antonine Wall (142), a war in Mauretania (145-152) and minor troubles in Dacia, Egypt and among the Brigantes. He never left Italy during his reign, governing from Rome and his villa at Lorium, and relied on long-serving governors and friends. He left a surplus of 2.7 billion sesterces. He named his daughter Faustina's husband, Marcus, as heir, granting him tribunician power in 147. His wife Faustina the Elder died in 140, and he founded the alimentary scheme of the puellae Faustinianae in her honour. Legal measures of his reign favoured slaves and the presumption of liberty, and jurists such as Volusius Maecianus and Gaius were active. He celebrated Rome's 900th anniversary in 148. Aelius Aristides delivered his Roman Oration under him, praising the empire as a world city. He died at Lorium on 7 March 161 after eating Alpine cheese, giving the watchword "aequanimitas". Marcus Aurelius's tribute in Meditations 1.16 is the fullest portrait of a good ruler in ancient literature. The scarcity of narrative sources (Dio's account is lost) makes the reign appear uneventful, which modern historians see as both a reality and an illusion.

Marcus Annius Verus, born in Rome on 26 April 121 to a rich Spanish family, grandson of the three-times consul Annius Verus, was noticed by Hadrian, who called him "Verissimus". In 138, aged seventeen, he was adopted by Antoninus at Hadrian's command, becoming Marcus Aelius Aurelius Verus, was made Caesar in 139, married Antoninus's daughter Faustina in 145, received tribunician power in 147, and was trained in government for over twenty years. His teachers included Fronto in Latin rhetoric, Herodes Atticus in Greek and the Stoics Junius Rusticus and Apollonius of Chalcedon; at about 25 he turned decisively to philosophy. On succeeding in 161 he made Lucius Verus co-emperor. His reign was dominated by crises: the Parthian invasion of Armenia and Syria, the Roman counter-offensive (162-166), the Antonine Plague brought back by the army, the invasion of Italy by Marcomanni and Quadi (170), the long Marcomannic wars along the Danube (166-180) that kept him at the front for most of his last fourteen years, the revolt of Avidius Cassius (175) and the death of Faustina. He financed the wars by auctioning palace treasures rather than raising taxes, recruited slaves and gladiators, settled barbarians within the empire and debased the coinage. He was conscientious in jurisdiction, generous to the Senate and patron of Athens' philosophical schools. Christians suffered in local persecutions, including the martyrs of Lyon (177), though there was no imperial persecution policy. He made his son Commodus co-Augustus in 177 and died on the Danube front on 17 March 180, possibly of plague. His Meditations, written in Greek as private notes for self-examination, are the last great work of Stoicism and present the struggle of a ruler to live by reason, duty and acceptance of mortality. The Column of Marcus Aurelius and the Capitoline equestrian statue survive. Dio and Herodian celebrate him as the best emperor; his choice of Commodus as successor has been criticised since antiquity.

Lucius Ceionius Commodus, born on 15 December 130, son of Hadrian's first chosen heir Lucius Aelius Caesar, was adopted by Antoninus in 138 according to Hadrian's plan, together with Marcus Aurelius, but was given no title as Caesar and held a single consulship (154) before his elevation. On Antoninus's death in 161, Marcus insisted that Lucius be made co-emperor with equal titles as Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus, the first formal joint rule. When the Parthian king Vologases IV invaded Armenia and destroyed a Roman army at Elegeia (161) and defeated the governor of Syria, Lucius was sent east in 162 as commander, travelling slowly and enjoying himself at Corinth, Athens and Antioch, and at the resort of Daphne, where he was accused of debauchery. The campaigns were directed by his generals, Statius Priscus, who took Artaxata (163), Avidius Cassius, who captured Seleucia and Ctesiphon (165) and invaded Media (166), and Martius Verus. Lucius took the titles Armeniacus, Parthicus Maximus and Medicus and celebrated a triumph with Marcus in October 166. He married Marcus's daughter Lucilla at Ephesus in 164. His army brought back the plague. He then went with Marcus to the northern front in 168, and on the return to Rome early in 169 he died of a stroke (apoplexy) near Altinum, aged 38; he was deified. The Historia Augusta portrays him as a pleasure-loving playboy who turned his house into a tavern, kept a golden statue of his favourite horse Volucer and fed it raisins and nuts; this portrait is coloured by the biographer's fictions, though Fronto's letters show genuine affection between Lucius, his tutor and Marcus. Rumours that Marcus or Faustina poisoned him have no basis. Modern historians (Birley) present him as a loyal, if lightweight, colleague who did what was required of him as figurehead commander.

Lucius Aurelius Commodus, born at Lanuvium on 31 August 161 with a twin brother who died at four, was the first emperor born to a reigning emperor since Titus. Made Caesar in 166, he accompanied his father to the Danube, received the toga virilis in 175, tribunician power and the title Augustus in 177 and married Bruttia Crispina in 178. On Marcus's death in March 180 he became sole emperor at eighteen, and against the advice of his father's generals quickly made peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi, returning to Rome, a decision the sources blame on his laziness but which may have been prudent. The conspiracy of his sister Lucilla in 182, in which an assassin cried "the Senate sends you this" as he struck, poisoned his relations with the Senate. He left government to favourites: the praetorian prefect Perennis, who dominated until 185 when soldiers from Britain secured his execution, then the freedman Cleander, who sold offices and was sacrificed to the mob during a grain riot in 190. Commodus's reign saw wars in Britain and Dacia, the "War of the Deserters" led by Maternus in Gaul and Spain, a plot that nearly killed him at the Megalensia (187), the return of the plague (189) and fires. In his last years he identified himself with Hercules, renamed the months after his twelve names, called Rome Colonia Commodiana, and fought in the arena as a secutor, killing animals and gladiators; Dio was an eyewitness. He was strangled in his bath on 31 December 192 by the athlete Narcissus in a plot organised by his mistress Marcia, the chamberlain Eclectus and the prefect Laetus. The Senate condemned his memory, but Septimius Severus deified him in 195 to legitimise his own claimed descent from Marcus. Dio's judgement that his accession marked the descent from an age of gold to one of iron set the tradition. Modern historians (Hekster) see his self-presentation as a deliberate, if extreme, strategy to appeal to the people and the army over the Senate.

Gaius Avidius Cassius was born c. 130 at Cyrrhus in Syria, son of Gaius Avidius Heliodorus, an orator from Egypt who became Hadrian's secretary for Greek correspondence and prefect of Egypt; he claimed descent from the Seleucids. Entering the Senate, he made his name as legate of III Gallica in the Parthian war under Lucius Verus, leading the advance down the Euphrates, winning a battle at Dura-Europos, and capturing Seleucia and Ctesiphon in 165, where Seleucia was sacked despite opening its gates, and invading Media in 166. He became consul (166) and governor of Syria and received a special command over the whole East, known from inscriptions, which made him the most powerful man after the emperors. He suppressed the Bucoli revolt in Egypt (172). Dio describes him as a stern disciplinarian, who crucified deserters and cut off the hands of soldiers who attacked the enemy without orders. In April 175, apparently having received false news of Marcus's death on the Danube, and according to rumour encouraged by Faustina, who feared for her son Commodus's succession if Marcus died, he proclaimed himself emperor. He was recognised in Syria, Egypt and much of the East, though not in Cappadocia, held by Martius Verus. When it became clear that Marcus was alive and marching east, his support collapsed; after three months and six days he was killed by a centurion and a decurion, who sent his head to Marcus. Marcus refused to see it, burned Cassius's correspondence unread and pardoned most of his supporters, though the Senate punished some. Dio's sympathetic picture of Marcus's clemency contrasts with the Historia Augusta's life, which contains forged letters. Modern historians debate whether Faustina was involved and whether the revolt was an honest mistake or a long-planned attempt to secure power against the young Commodus.
set.debate: Whether the revolt arose from a false report of Marcus's death, and whether Faustina encouraged it.

set.detail: Jesus (Yeshua) of Nazareth was born c. 6-4 BC, probably in Nazareth in Galilee (the gospels of Matthew and Luke set his birth at Bethlehem), to Mary and Joseph, a craftsman (tekton); he had brothers, including James, and sisters. Around 28 he was baptised by John the Baptist and, after John's arrest, began preaching the imminent kingdom of God in Galilee, especially around Capernaum and the Sea of Galilee, gathering disciples, including an inner circle of twelve, symbolising the restoration of Israel, among them Peter, Andrew, James and John. He acquired fame as a healer and exorcist, taught in parables, shared meals with tax collectors and sinners, emphasised love of God and neighbour, forgiveness and the reversal of status, and debated the interpretation of the Torah with Pharisees and scribes. He went to Jerusalem for Passover around 30 or 33, where his entry and action in the Temple, overturning the tables of money changers, alarmed the priestly authorities. After a final meal with his disciples, he was arrested at night, examined by the High Priest Caiaphas and handed to the prefect Pontius Pilate, who had him crucified as "King of the Jews". His followers soon proclaimed that God had raised him from the dead and that he would return as messiah and Lord. The main sources are the four gospels (c. 70-100) and Paul's letters (c. 50-60), with references in Josephus (Antiquities 18.63-64, 20.200) and Tacitus (Annals 15.44); later rabbinic and pagan references are polemical. The "quest for the historical Jesus" since Reimarus and Schweitzer has produced varying portraits: apocalyptic prophet (Schweitzer, Sanders, Ehrman), Jewish sage or Cynic-like teacher (Crossan), social reformer or charismatic healer (Vermes). Almost all historians accept that he existed, was baptised by John, preached in Galilee and was crucified under Pilate. The movement he founded spread rapidly through the eastern Mediterranean and reached Rome by the 40s.
set.debate: Reconstructions of the historical Jesus: apocalyptic prophet, sage, reformer or healer.

set.detail: Paul (Saul), born c. 5 in Tarsus in Cilicia to a Jewish family of the tribe of Benjamin, was, according to Acts, a Roman citizen by birth, trained as a Pharisee in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and worked as a tentmaker. He persecuted the followers of Jesus until a vision of the risen Christ near Damascus c. 33-36 made him an apostle to the Gentiles. After time in Arabia (Nabataea), Damascus and a first visit to Peter and James in Jerusalem, he worked for about fourteen years in Syria and Cilicia, then with Barnabas in Cyprus and southern Galatia. At the Jerusalem council (c. 48-49) he won recognition that Gentile converts need not be circumcised, and he confronted Peter at Antioch over table fellowship. In the years c. 49-57 he founded churches in Galatia, Macedonia (Philippi, Thessalonica), Achaea (Corinth, where he appeared before Gallio c. 51-52) and Asia (Ephesus), and organised a collection for the poor of Jerusalem. His seven undisputed letters (1 Thessalonians, Galatians, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, Philemon, Romans) are the earliest Christian writings and set out his theology: justification by faith in Christ rather than by works of the Law, the inclusion of Gentiles in Israel's promises, the church as the body of Christ, and the imminent return of the Lord. Arrested in the Temple in Jerusalem c. 57, held for two years at Caesarea under Felix, he appealed to Caesar before Festus and was sent to Rome, shipwrecked on Malta on the way, and lived under house arrest in Rome for two years. Christian tradition says he was beheaded on the Via Ostia under Nero, c. 62-67. Colossians, Ephesians, 2 Thessalonians and the Pastorals are widely considered later works in his name. His interpretation has been central to Christian theology (Augustine, Luther) and to modern debates (the "New Perspective" of Sanders, Dunn and Wright) about his relationship to Judaism.

Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 BC near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul to a landowning family, educated at Cremona, Milan and Rome, and studied Epicurean philosophy with Siro at Naples. His first work, the Eclogues (c. 42-38 BC), ten pastoral poems modelled on Theocritus, reflected the land confiscations for veterans after Philippi (the first eclogue alludes to the loss and recovery of land) and included the "messianic" fourth eclogue prophesying the birth of a child who would bring a golden age, later read by Christians as a prophecy of Christ. Through Asinius Pollio and Maecenas he entered Octavian's circle and introduced Horace to Maecenas. The Georgics (c. 29 BC), four books on farming, bees and the story of Orpheus, dedicated to Maecenas, were read to Octavian on his return from the East. He then spent eleven years on the Aeneid, the national epic of Rome in twelve books, telling of Aeneas's flight from Troy, his love affair with Dido at Carthage, his descent to the underworld, where he sees the future heroes of Rome, and his war in Latium against Turnus. The poem combines Homeric models with Roman history and Augustan ideology, while expressing the suffering and cost of empire. Virgil went to Greece in 19 BC to revise it, met Augustus at Athens, fell ill at Megara and died at Brundisium on 21 September 19 BC; he asked for the unfinished poem to be burned, but Augustus had it published by Varius and Tucca. He was buried near Naples. Shy, unmarried and reputedly called "Parthenias" (the virgin), he became the central author of Latin education; the Aeneid was quoted on Pompeian walls and studied for centuries, and in the Middle Ages he was seen as a sage and magician, Dante's guide through Hell and Purgatory. Modern criticism debates the "two voices" of the Aeneid, celebration and pessimism.

Publius Ovidius Naso was born on 20 March 43 BC at Sulmo in the Paelignian country to an old equestrian family; he studied rhetoric in Rome under Arellius Fuscus and Porcius Latro, toured Greece and Asia Minor, held minor judicial posts and abandoned a senatorial career for poetry. Patronised by Messalla Corvinus, he became the leading poet of Rome after the deaths of Virgil, Tibullus and Propertius. His elegiac works include the Amores (love poems to "Corinna"), the Heroides (letters from mythological heroines to absent lovers), the Ars Amatoria (a mock-didactic manual of seduction, c. 2 BC-AD 2), the Remedia Amoris and the Medicamina Faciei Femineae (on cosmetics). His masterpiece, the Metamorphoses, fifteen books of hexameter tales of transformation from the creation of the world to the apotheosis of Julius Caesar and the reign of Augustus, was completed by AD 8, as was half of the Fasti, a poetic calendar of Roman festivals. In AD 8 Augustus suddenly relegated him (keeping his property and citizenship) to Tomis on the Black Sea, citing "a poem and a mistake" (carmen et error): the poem was the Ars Amatoria, while the mistake remains a mystery, often linked to the adultery scandal of Augustus's granddaughter Julia the Younger, exiled the same year. In exile he wrote the Tristia and the Epistulae ex Ponto, laments and appeals to friends and to Augustus and Tiberius, describing the cold, the Getae, the dangers of raids and his learning of the Getic language, in which he claimed to have written a poem. He was never recalled and died at Tomis in AD 17 or 18. His influence on European literature and art, through the Metamorphoses as a source for mythology, has been immense, from Chaucer and Shakespeare to Titian and Bernini. Some scholars have even questioned whether the exile was real, a minority view.

Aelius (or Claudius) Galenus was born in Pergamum in 129, son of a wealthy architect, Nicon, who directed him to medicine after a dream. He studied philosophy and medicine in Pergamum, Smyrna, Corinth and Alexandria, where he learned anatomy from skeletons, then served as physician to the gladiators of the high priest of Asia at Pergamum (157-161), gaining experience of wounds and diet. In 162 he went to Rome, where his public anatomical dissections and vivisections, his cures of aristocrats such as the philosopher Eudemus and the consul Flavius Boethus, and his polemics with rival medical sects made him famous and controversial. He left Rome in 166 as the plague arrived, but was summoned by Marcus and Lucius to Aquileia in 168-169 and became court physician, looking after the young Commodus and preparing the theriac antidote for Marcus. He spent the rest of his life in Rome, surviving into the reign of Septimius Severus and possibly Caracalla, dying c. 216, though some sources say later. His output was enormous, around 500 works, of which some 150 survive in Greek, Arabic or Latin, about 3 million words, covering anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, diagnosis, prognosis, hygiene, and philosophy (logic, ethics and the soul). He combined Hippocratic humoral theory with Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy and his own experimental work, demonstrating that arteries carry blood, not air, the functions of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and spinal cord, and the role of the kidneys. His descriptions of the Antonine Plague are the main medical source for it. The rediscovered treatise On Avoiding Distress (found in Thessaloniki in 2005) describes his losses of books, drugs and instruments in the fire of 192. Translated into Syriac and Arabic by Hunayn ibn Ishaq and others, and then into Latin, his works dominated medicine in Europe and the Islamic world until Vesalius and Harvey.
